pr_title: Creating new TypeName without reparsing + usage in NRBF
pr_body:
@jkotas I've tried to implement the APIs we have discussed in #102263 and so far it looks good.

I need to spend more time testing `MakeGenericTypeName` and thinking about all edge cases.

contributes to #102263
fixes #106022
pr_comments:
Note regarding the `new-api-needs-documentation` label:

    This serves as a reminder for when your PR is modifying a ref *.cs file and adding/modifying public APIs, please make sure the API implementation in the src *.cs file is documented with triple slash comments, so the PR reviewers can sign off that change.

    This serves as a reminder for when your PR is modifying a ref *.cs file and adding/modifying public APIs, please make sure the API implementation in the src *.cs file is documented with triple slash comments, so the PR reviewers can sign off that change.

> I need to spend more time testing `MakeGenericTypeName` and thinking about all edge cases.

The `MakeGenericType` name from reflection works only for generic type definitions:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/9e57de2b2a71b449057ffe75823d332e44ffe8fa/src/coreclr/nativeaot/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Reflection/Runtime/TypeInfos/RuntimeTypeInfo.cs#L431

Should `MakeGenericTypeName` have similar limitation? Otherwise, we are going to allow for creating generic type names where `typeName.IsConstructedGenericType` is pointer, array etc. Such name would be illegal for runtimes we have today.

> Should MakeGenericTypeName have similar limitation? 

Sounds good to me. I assume that you are thinking about requiring `IsSimpleName` to be true. Correct?

> Sounds good to me. I assume that you are thinking about requiring `IsSimpleName` to be true. Correct?

`IsSimple` or `IsConstructedGenericType` (so users could change generic args of given generic type)

> IsConstructedGenericType (so users could change generic args of given generic type)

I do not think that regular reflection APIs allow this. Why would we want to allow it? If users want to change generic args of constructed generic type, they should get the generic type definition first on their side.

> fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/102263

This is missing `CreateSimpleTypeName` API from this proposal.

issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: TypeName.MakeSimpleTypeName(AssemblyNameInfo) to avoid type name reparsing
comments:
> I can not use the approved TypeName.CreateSimpleTypeName because it expects unescaped input. 

I think you can use it. I agree that `TypeName.CreateSimpleTypeName` is a less efficient in the BF use case when compared to the API proposed here, but there is no fundamental problem doing what the BF needs to achieve using the approved APIs.

review_comments: `FullName` can produce non-linear amount of work in case a long assembly name was applied to multiple generic arguments. Is it a concern? Should we omit the `FullName` in the exception message?
The NrbfDecoder won't ever call this method for non-simple types, so I believe it's acceptable.

I do not have a problem with it. 

I think you need to be careful in the threat-modeling about any place (including logging or error handling) that gets the full name since it may produce non-linear amount of work. Reducing the number of places that get the full name can make this easier. It is sort of defense-in-depth.

Exception messages, particularly for this library, are an interesting beast.

The only writer I know of for NRBF is BF (and the remote procedure call parts of remoting, but it doesn't save answers).  BF won't mangle type names (more than it already does), and won't write down unsupported records (or we would have supported them).  So, where is the person getting this bad data other than from corrupted/tampered/malicious data?  They probably don't care what kind of record isn't supported, it just means the data's bad.  They probably don't care what the invalid type name was, it just means the data's bad.

Someone trying to write a new NRBF writer might end up caring, so we shouldn't discard the data, but it could easily be stored in either the property bag or a named property on a new derived exception type (if we felt it needed it), and the 0.01% who actually want the data can get it, while the 99.99% who don't care don't ever have to worry about the safety of logging exception messages.

A nicer middle ground is to capture numeric/enummy things in the message, but leave things like "arbitrary text" out.

Oh, right, this then takes the string and does further work (TypeName.Parse) before squirrelling it away in the array.

OK, this is probably the better approach.
